note: A USDA hardiness zone describes average annual extreme minimum WINTER temperature — it is a winter-survival rating for perennials, not a frost-date band. The frost dates below are widely-used approximations for each zone, not official USDA figures, and a single zone spans hundreds of miles. Treat them as a default guess and replace them with your own local averages wherever you have them.
source: Zone temperature bands: USDA Plant Hardiness Zone Map, 2023 revision. Frost dates: conventional per-zone approximations, to be superseded by station-level data from NOAA NCEI 1991-2020 Climate Normals (which also give the 40%, 30%, 20% and 10% freeze-probability dates) or your county cooperative extension office.

zones.regions: Northern Minnesota, northern North Dakota, interior Alaska, high-elevation Rockies
zones.summary: One of the shortest growing seasons in the continental US. Short-season varieties and transplants matter more here than anywhere else.

zones.regions: Minnesota, Wisconsin, northern Michigan, Vermont, Maine, Montana
zones.summary: A real but tight season. Tomatoes and peppers need an indoor head start to ripen before the September frost.

zones.regions: Iowa, Nebraska, Illinois, Ohio, upstate New York, Massachusetts, Colorado Front Range
zones.summary: Comfortable for nearly every beginner crop, with room for a spring planting and a fall planting of greens.

zones.regions: Kansas City, St. Louis, Philadelphia, southern New England, Pacific Northwest interior
zones.summary: Roughly six frost-free months. You can plant a spring crop, a summer crop, and a fall crop of the same bed.

zones.regions: Virginia, Tennessee, Oklahoma, northern Georgia, Seattle, Portland
zones.summary: Seven months frost-free. Mid-summer heat, not frost, becomes the limiting factor for lettuce and spinach.

zones.regions: Atlanta, Dallas, Austin, coastal Carolinas, central California, Willamette Valley
zones.summary: Eight frost-free months, but July and August are hostile to cool-season crops. Plant greens in fall and late winter instead of summer.

zones.regions: Houston, Orlando, Phoenix, coastal Southern California
zones.summary: Nearly year-round growing, with an inverted calendar: winter is the prime season for greens and root crops, summer is the hard part.

zones.regions: South Florida, Florida Keys, Hawaii, southernmost coastal California
zones.summary: Effectively frost-free. Treat the cool months as your main season and skip cool-season crops entirely from June through September.
